Maximal standard length in the Trinidadian guppy lineage HP Marianne91 has been quantified in laboratory-maintained cohorts at a stable water temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], with the largest individuals attaining a total length of 3.73 cm [Li = 3.73 cm]. This value, recorded from the tip of the snout to the end of the caudal fin, represents the upper boundary of somatic growth under controlled conditions where food was provided ad libitum. Such a maximum standard length of 3.73 cm [Li = 3.73 cm] aligns well with the modest body sizes characteristic of Poecilia reticulata from low-elevation Trinidadian streams, where compact body plans are favoured in habitats with high flow variability at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. The thermal regime of 26 °C [T = 26 °C] under which these measurements were obtained corresponds closely to the mean annual water temperature of the Marianne River source population, ensuring that the recorded length is ecologically relevant rather than a laboratory artefact.

Comparisons of developmental timing under contrasting nutritional regimes reveal considerable plasticity in the Trinidadian guppy HP Mrn91. When reared at a constant temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C] and supplied with a high-quantity diet, parturition occurred at a mean age of 22.5 days [ab = 22.5 days], indicating that abundant food resources accelerate prenatal development and reduce gestation length. This mean age at birth of 22.5 days [ab = 22.5 days] under high food conditions is notably shorter than the gestation periods reported for many other live-bearing poeciliids of comparable body size, suggesting that HP Marianne91 has evolved a relatively rapid developmental trajectory at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. The increased mean age at birth under low food of 23.0666667 days [ab = 23.0666667 days] represents a measurable delay in parturition relative to the well-fed cohort, a response that likely allows embryos additional time to acquire and store essential yolk reserves before the constraints of reduced maternal provisioning take effect at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This nutritional plasticity in developmental timing underscores the species' ability to modulate prenatal investment in response to resource availability, a trait that may enhance offspring viability under fluctuating stream conditions.

Critical differences emerged when we examined the interaction between maternal nutritional state and the thermal environment on offspring production. At the standardised rearing temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the mean age at birth for females in the high food treatment was 22.5 days [ab = 22.5 days], a value that reflects the maximal developmental speed possible under these permissive conditions. Such nutritional sensitivity in the mean age at birth may carry important consequences for offspring quality and subsequent juvenile survival in variable stream environments.

Reproductive output in the Trinidadian guppy HP Marianne91, when examined under controlled laboratory conditions, further underscores the species' capacity for rapid population turnover. At the constant temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C] used throughout this study, the mean age at birth among well-fed females was 22.5 days [ab = 22.5 days], a remarkably short interval that allows multiple broods to be produced within a single breeding season. When food resources were limited, the mean age at birth increased to 23.0666667 days [ab = 23.0666667 days] at the same 26 °C [T = 26 °C] regime, indicating that even under nutritional stress, females retain the ability to produce viable offspring with only a minor extension of gestation. Within the broader life-history strategy of this Trinidadian guppy line, the interplay between somatic growth and reproductive timing is particularly instructive. The maximum standard length of 3.73 cm [Li = 3.73 cm], achieved under the consistent thermal baseline of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], delineates the upper boundary of body size that can be supported by the local resource base and predation regime. At this same temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the mean age at birth for females on a high food ration was 22.5 days [ab = 22.5 days], while those on a low food ration produced broods at a mean age of 23.0666667 days [ab = 23.0666667 days].
